title: Nacogdoches Will Weigh a Drive-Through at Appleby Sand and Stallings. The Public Hearing Is Tuesday
thumbnailMessage: A residential corner could become a drive-through site
summary: Nacogdoches City Council is scheduled to consider rezoning a 0.35-acre residential parcel for local-business use and approving an eating place with a drive-through at Appleby Sand Road and NE Stallings Drive.
content:
A small corner parcel in north Nacogdoches is headed for a consequential land-use vote Tuesday. The City Council is scheduled to consider two linked requests for approximately 0.35 acres at the southeast corner of Appleby Sand Road and NE Stallings Drive: a change from R-1 single-family zoning to B-1 local business, and a specific-use permit for an eating place with a drive-through.

The public hearing is set for 5:30 p.m. Aug. 18 in City Council Chambers, Room 119, at Nacogdoches City Hall, 202 E. Pilar Street. The city identifies the property as Nacogdoches Central Appraisal District parcel 1000004518, Lot 74 in City Block 54.

Those identifiers matter because they let residents distinguish the actual request from rumor about a larger tract or a different intersection. A commercial real-estate record for the same parcel independently describes it as a 0.35-acre corner lot at FM 2609, also known as Appleby Sand Road, and NE Stallings Drive. The city notice does not identify a restaurant brand, operator or final tenant. Until the applicant or city publishes that information, residents should not fill the gap with guesses.

The two votes also should not be collapsed into one. The zoning case, ZON2026-06, asks whether the parcel should move from single-family residential to local-business zoning. The specific-use case, SUP2026-06, asks whether a drive-through eating place should be allowed on that parcel if the business zoning is approved. Council members can evaluate the underlying commercial designation and the particular drive-through use as separate questions.

Nacogdoches says its Planning and Zoning Commission makes recommendations to the City Council on zoning changes and that both bodies must hold public hearings when zoning regulations or districts are amended. The commission meeting was scheduled for Aug. 10. As of Saturday morning, the city's public project notice did not state the commission's recommendation or post a final council staff report for the Aug. 18 decision. The council record should make that recommendation, the vote and any conditions easy to find before deliberation.

For nearby residents and drivers, the most useful questions are concrete. Where would vehicles enter and exit? How many cars can queue on the site without spilling toward the intersection? Would a left turn be allowed from both roads? What hours are proposed? Where would menu boards, lighting, trash service and delivery vehicles sit? What screening would separate the use from any nearby homes?

The parcel's size makes those details especially important. A 0.35-acre site is about 15,000 square feet, and a drive-through must fit the building, parking, circulation, fire access, utilities, landscaping and vehicle queue into that area. A concept can satisfy a broad land-use label and still require careful engineering before it functions safely. Council should separate the policy decision from later technical permits while refusing to treat those technical questions as somebody else's problem.

Traffic deserves a record rather than a slogan. Appleby Sand Road and NE Stallings Drive carry ordinary neighborhood traffic along with school, work and commercial trips. A drive-through could add convenience and economic activity. It could also concentrate turning movements at busy periods. The responsible test is not whether one side calls the project growth and the other calls it congestion. It is whether a traffic plan shows safe access, adequate sight distance and enough internal stacking for the proposed operating pattern.

The city's zoning materials explain that Planning and Zoning is a quasi-judicial body and that its meetings are open to the public. That means comments are most useful when tied to the standards in the ordinance and to evidence about the site. Supporters can point to compatibility, services, access and economic use. Opponents can point to traffic, noise, light, drainage, buffering or residential impacts. Personal attacks and speculation about an unnamed operator do not help the council make a defensible decision.

Council should disclose every condition attached to an approval. A specific-use permit can be more accountable than a broad promise because enforceable conditions can address hours, access, screening, lighting, signs, outdoor speakers, trash pickup or other site-specific concerns. But a condition only protects the public if it is precise, recorded and monitored. Vague assurances made at the podium should not substitute for language in the ordinance or permit.

The city should also explain what happens if one request passes and the other fails. If council approves B-1 zoning but rejects the drive-through permit, residents need to know which other B-1 uses could be allowed later without another rezoning case. If the permit is approved subject to a particular site plan, the public should be able to see whether a future redesign would require additional review.

Property owners near a zoning case have a direct interest, but the hearing belongs to the full city. Land-use decisions create precedents about where commercial activity belongs, how transitions from homes to businesses are handled and how much information the public receives before a vote. Consistency matters: a council should be able to explain how the same standards would apply to a different applicant at a different intersection.

Residents who want to speak should verify the city's current agenda and public-comment procedure before Tuesday. The Planning and Zoning page lists the department's phone number as 936-559-2571, and the city meeting calendar lists the council session at City Hall. Written comments should identify ZON2026-06 and SUP2026-06 so they enter the correct file.

The best outcome is not predetermined by the word restaurant, residential or growth. It comes from a transparent record, a site plan that answers predictable safety and compatibility questions, and a vote that states why the proposal meets or fails the city's standards. Nacogdoches residents have a short window to inspect the request. The council has an obligation to make the facts visible before it changes the map.
